title: Raising Capital: What the Choice of Instrument Tells You
summary: Companies raise money in a rough order of preference, and departures from that order are informative.

lesson.body:
A company needing capital has a menu, ordered roughly from cheapest and least intrusive to most expensive and most dilutive.

**Internal cash.** No issuance costs, no disclosure, no new claims. Always first if available.

**Bank debt.** A relationship lender, a small number of counterparties, covenants, and speed. Renegotiable if things go wrong, which is a real advantage.

**Bond issuance.** Larger, longer, usually looser covenants, and a dispersed group of holders. Cheaper for a good credit and far harder to renegotiate — coordinating hundreds of bondholders is a genuine obstacle in a restructuring.

**Private credit.** A single lender or small club, faster and more flexible than a bond, more expensive, and increasingly the default for mid-sized borrowers.

**Equity.** Most expensive in [[required-return|required return]], permanently dilutive, and the only form that absorbs losses without a covenant. In a crisis it is often the only option available.

**The order matters because departures from it are informative.** A company issuing equity when it could have borrowed is telling you something — about its own view of its share price, about its debt capacity, or about what its lenders said.

**Issuance is a signal, because management knows more about the company than the market does.**

The logic is clean. Managers who believe their shares are undervalued will not want to issue them cheaply — they will borrow instead. Managers who believe their shares are overvalued face the opposite incentive.

So the market reasonably reads an equity issue as a statement about price, which is why announcements of new equity are so often met with a falling share price. The company may have excellent reasons; the market applies the inference anyway.

Three readings worth knowing:

**Equity raised at a low price for growth** — either a genuine opportunity the company cannot fund otherwise, or debt capacity that has run out. Ask which.

**Equity raised into a strong share price** — reasonable capital management, and the timing rewards the company at the expense of new holders.

**Equity raised in a hurry after a covenant discussion** — the lenders required it. The most informative of the three, and rarely described that way.

**And the same logic applies to a private company's funding round.** A flat or down round is not just a valuation event; it is information about what better-informed parties would pay.

**The identity of the lender matters as much as the terms, and it is decided at issuance rather than in a crisis.**

This is the practical lesson of the last two credit cycles, and it is easy to miss because it sounds administrative.

**A relationship bank** has an incentive to work with a borrower through a difficult period, because it wants the future business and it holds the loan on its own book. Renegotiation is a conversation.

**A syndicate of bondholders** has no relationship and no shared interest. Some bought at par and some at 60. Their incentives differ, and getting a consent threshold is slow and expensive.

**A private credit fund** is one counterparty with the authority to amend and a strong interest in avoiding a write-down. Amendments are fast — and the fund also holds the equity's fate in a very small number of hands.

**A distressed buyer who bought your debt in the secondary market** wants the company, not the coupon. Their optimal outcome may be a restructuring that wipes out the equity, and nothing prevents them buying in.

**So the question at issuance is: if this goes wrong, who is on the other side of the table, and what do they want?** That answer is chosen when the debt is raised and cannot be changed afterwards — the debt can be traded to anyone.

lesson.caption: What each instrument costs and constrains
rows: Disclosure, near-impossible renegotiation, and the debt can be bought by anyone.
Higher coupon, and a single counterparty with a great deal of influence.
Pricing, and the whole structure sits with one party.
Absorbs losses, no maturity, no covenant
Permanent dilution, highest required return, and a signal to the market.

lesson.body: A company with [[ebitda|EBITDA]] of 80 and existing debt of 400 needs 100 for an acquisition. Consider three routes.
walkthrough: **More debt.** Debt becomes 500, leverage 500/80 = **6.25x** from 5.0x. Interest at 5% adds 5, taking interest to 25 and EBITDA coverage from 4.0x to **3.2x**.
**Equity.** Leverage falls to 400/80 = 5.0x on a larger business, and existing shareholders are diluted. No new fixed obligation.
**A mix — 50 of each.** Leverage 450/80 = **5.6x**, coverage 80/22.5 = **3.6x**, and half the dilution.

Now the question that decides it: **what does the acquisition add to EBITDA?** If it adds 20, the debt route gives leverage of 500/100 = **5.0x** — unchanged from today, and the deal is self-financing in leverage terms.

**Read that carefully: the same 100 of debt takes leverage to 6.25x or leaves it at 5.0x depending entirely on what is being bought.** Financing decisions cannot be assessed apart from what the money does.

Sanity check worth reusing: **compute pro forma leverage including the acquired EBITDA, then compute it excluding the acquired EBITDA.** The gap is how much of the structure's safety depends on the acquisition performing as promised — which is the risk being taken, stated as a number.

lesson.body:
**Pro forma leverage that assumes the synergies.** A structure sized on post-synergy EBITDA is levered on a forecast. If the synergies are late, the leverage is real and the earnings are not.

**Refinancing risk clustered on one date.** Raising everything at once is efficient and creates a single point of failure. Laddered maturities cost a little more and remove that.

**Ignoring who can buy the debt.** Publicly traded loans and bonds can be accumulated by a distressed investor whose objective is the equity. This is a known route to control and it is available to anyone.

**Equity issued at the bottom.** Companies that most need equity can raise it least attractively. The cheapest time to raise equity is when it is not needed, and that argument rarely wins against dilution objections.

**Covenant-lite as an unambiguous win for the borrower.** Fewer tests means fewer early conversations, and it also means a lender who first engages when the situation is much worse — and with less goodwill.

**Currency mismatch.** Borrowing in a currency the revenue is not earned in adds an exposure that has nothing to do with the business, and it has ended more emerging-market companies than any operational failure.

**In a competitive acquisition process, certainty of financing is worth real money to a seller — which is why the cheapest financing frequently loses.**

A seller choosing between two bids weighs price against the probability of completion. A bid backed by a signed private credit commitment can be preferred over a higher bid dependent on a bond syndication that may not clear.

This is the main reason private credit took share from the syndicated market: not price, which is worse, but **certainty and speed**. A borrower pays a premium for a commitment that does not depend on market conditions between signing and closing.

The consequence worth understanding as an investor: **that premium is the return in a [[direct-lending|direct lending]] fund.** It is compensation for providing certainty and for holding an illiquid loan — which is a genuine service and a genuine risk, not an anomaly.

It also means the direct lending return should compress when syndicated markets are functioning smoothly and widen when they are not. **A manager reporting a stable spread through a full cycle is either exceptionally disciplined or not marking to the market they operate in.**

**Ask for pro forma leverage with and without the acquired or forecast EBITDA.** The gap is the portion of safety that depends on a plan.

**Ask who holds the debt and whether it can be traded.** If a distressed buyer accumulates it, your counterparty's objective changes entirely and nothing prevents that.

**Ask for the maturity ladder.** Everything due on one date is a single point of failure with a known deadline.

**When a company raises equity, ask what its lenders said first.** An equity raise following a covenant conversation is a different event from one funding an opportunity, and the announcement rarely distinguishes them.

**For a direct lending manager, ask how the spread has moved with syndicated market conditions.** A spread that never moves suggests the pricing is not being tested.

items: Companies raise capital in a rough order — internal cash, bank debt, bonds, private credit, equity — and departures from that order are informative about debt capacity and about management's view of its own price.

The identity of the lender is chosen at issuance and cannot be changed afterwards: a relationship bank negotiates, a bond syndicate cannot coordinate, and a distressed buyer of your debt may want the equity.
The same 100 of debt takes leverage to 6.25x or leaves it at 5.0x depending on what the money buys. Financing cannot be assessed apart from use.
Private credit's premium is payment for certainty and speed, not a market inefficiency — which means the spread should widen and compress with syndicated market conditions.

questions.stem: EBITDA 80, existing debt 400. The company borrows another 100. What is pro forma leverage, in turns, before any acquired earnings?
questions.explanation: This is the honest starting point, because the acquired earnings are a forecast until they arrive. Comparing it with leverage including the acquisition — 5.0x if the target adds 20 of EBITDA — brackets the risk being taken.

questions.stem: Interest was 20 and the new 100 of debt costs 5%. What is EBITDA interest coverage after the raise, using EBITDA of 80? Two decimal places.
questions.explanation: From 4.0x to 3.2x on a 25% increase in debt — coverage degrades faster than leverage rises, because the interest is added to a denominator that was already substantial. Coverage is the more sensitive measure and the one closer to an actual payment.

questions.stem: Why do share prices often fall when a company announces an equity issue?
choices: Because the new shares are always issued at a discount
Because management knows more than the market, so issuing equity is read as a view that the shares are not cheap
Because equity is more expensive than debt
Because regulators require a price adjustment
rationales: Discounts are common and are a mechanism rather than the underlying reason for the reaction.
Correct. A manager who believed the shares were cheap would prefer to borrow. Issuing them is therefore read as information about price, whatever the stated purpose.
The cost of equity is higher and that is known in advance and already in the price.
No such requirement exists; the move is a market reaction.
questions.explanation: The same inference runs through private markets: a flat or down funding round is information about what better-informed parties will pay, not merely an administrative repricing. It is why insiders participating pro rata in a down round is a meaningful signal in the other direction.

questions.stem: "Private credit is more expensive, so a rational borrower would always choose the syndicated market." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — borrowers pay the premium for certainty and speed, which in a competitive acquisition can be worth more than the coupon difference
False — private credit is actually cheaper than syndicated debt
True — the cheapest capital always wins
False — because syndicated markets are closed to most borrowers
rationales: Correct. A seller weighs price against the probability of completion, so a committed facility can win a deal that a market-dependent financing would lose. The premium buys that certainty.
It is generally more expensive, which is the premise of the question.
Cost is one dimension; speed, certainty, covenant flexibility and confidentiality are the others, and they are frequently decisive.
Access is genuinely restricted for smaller borrowers, and the choice exists for many who still pick private credit.
questions.explanation: Understanding the premium as payment for a service rather than as an inefficiency also tells you when it should compress: in calm markets where syndication is reliable, certainty is worth less. A direct lending spread that never moves with market conditions deserves a question.

questions.stem: Why does the identity of a company's lenders matter more in a downturn than the coupon does?
choices: Lenders can change the interest rate at will
Renegotiation depends on who is on the other side: a relationship bank negotiates, a bond syndicate struggles to coordinate, and a distressed buyer of the debt may want the equity
The coupon is not payable in a downturn
Lender identity determines the accounting treatment
rationales: Rates are contractual; what varies is willingness to amend the contract when the borrower needs it.

Correct. The debt can be traded to anyone, so the counterparty you negotiate with in year four may not be the one you signed with in year one — and their objective may be control rather than repayment.
It remains payable, which is precisely what makes the negotiation necessary.
Accounting treatment follows the instrument, not the holder.
questions.explanation: The practical implication at issuance: ask whether the debt is freely transferable and whether there are restrictions on who can hold it. Some borrowers negotiate lists of disqualified transferees for exactly this reason, and it is one of the more consequential clauses in a credit agreement.

questions.stem: A structure is sized at 5.5x leverage using post-synergy EBITDA. What is the risk?
choices: Post-synergy EBITDA is not a permitted basis for lending
If the synergies are late or smaller, the debt is real and the earnings supporting it are not — so actual leverage is higher than the structure was designed for
The interest rate will automatically rise
The covenant will be tested on a different measure
rationales: It is permitted and common, which is why the risk is worth naming rather than assuming away.
Correct. Leverage on today's actual EBITDA might be 6.5x or more. The structure assumes a delivery timetable, and delivery risk becomes credit risk.
Pricing is set at issuance; a margin ratchet moves with reported ratios rather than automatically.
Covenants are usually tested on a similarly adjusted measure, which is part of the same problem rather than a separate one.
questions.explanation: Always compute leverage on last-twelve-months reported EBITDA alongside the pro forma figure. The gap between them is the amount of the capital structure that rests on a plan, and it is the first number to revisit when the plan slips.
